analysis.title: Europe is selling more into the US AI build-out, but losing market share
key_insights: EU exports to the US of selected AI-infrastructure products rose from 2022 to the 12 months ending July 2026 by about €10bn (+55%) in electrical power equipment, €8bn (+77%) in compute hardware and €3bn (+30%) in cooling systems.

The product basket follows Waugh (2026) and includes servers, transformers and cooling equipment. The products are not exclusive to AI, so the figures do not identify exports destined for AI projects.
Europe's share of US imports in the selected basket rose to nearly 10% in early 2024, then fell to about 5.7% by July 2026.
The reversal began in 2024, before the broad US tariff increases on EU imports in 2025. It coincided with a change in the composition of US imports.
Compute and networking rose from roughly 54% of the basket in early 2024 to about 77% by July 2026. Europe has a small position in these categories, so their weight pulls down its aggregate share.
The EU share of US imports rose by about 1.6 percentage points in electrical power equipment and about 2 points in cooling, so European suppliers grew faster than those US import markets.
The EU share of US compute imports fell from roughly 4.5% to below 3%, even though compute became the second-largest contributor to EU export growth in the basket.
Europe's share of US networking imports fell by about 4 percentage points. Speciality materials show a large share fall but have little effect on the aggregate because of their small weight.

China's share of US imports in the basket fell from around 20% in 2020 to below 5%. Taiwan and Southeast Asia gained strongly, and Vietnam and Thailand account for more than 90% of Southeast Asia's increase since 2022.
China's lost share is not a direct transfer of orders to Europe. Customs data show country of origin, not manufacturer ownership or upstream component origin.

Production in computer and electronic products, electrical equipment and machinery (NACE C26-C28) is about 1.5% below its first-half 2022 level for the EU27, with Germany down about 9%. The Netherlands, Sweden and Hungary are up strongly, and the Netherlands gain is likely influenced by ASML and the semiconductor-equipment cluster.
These industries extend beyond AI-related equipment, so the production data cannot isolate the effect of US AI investment.

sector_views.rationale: European suppliers gained both exports and US import share in electrical power and cooling equipment, and US demand for these markets continues to expand.
The EU share of US compute imports fell from roughly 4.5% to below 3%, and its networking share fell about 4 percentage points.

macro_indicators.indicator: EU27 share of US imports in selected AI infrastructure basket
macro_indicators.reading: about 5.7% (July 2026), down from nearly 10% in early 2024
macro_indicators.interpretation: The aggregate share fell because compute and networking, where Europe has a small position, grew to a larger part of the basket.

macro_indicators.indicator: Compute and networking share of US basket imports
macro_indicators.reading: about 77%, up from roughly 54% in early 2024
macro_indicators.interpretation: The composition shift toward computing lowers Europe's aggregate share.

macro_indicators.indicator: EU27 production index (NACE C26-C28) vs first half 2022
macro_indicators.interpretation: Production gains from the US AI build-out are concentrated in particular locations, not visible across the EU as a whole.

risk_factors: Computing keeps taking a larger share of US AI imports, where European suppliers have a small and declining share.
Power and cooling markets grow more slowly than computing, so they account for a declining share of the total.
Production in the broader European industries remains below its early-2022 level, and gains are concentrated in a few countries.
geopolitical: US tariff increases on EU imports in 2025 are noted, but the report says the share reversal began in 2024, before the tariffs.
China's share of US AI-related imports fell from around 20% in 2020 to below 5%, with Taiwan and Southeast Asia gaining.

tension_points.theme: Europe's share of US AI imports
tension_points.bull_case: European exports of power, cooling and compute equipment to the US rose strongly since 2022, and European suppliers gained share in power and cooling.
tension_points.bear_case: The aggregate share fell from nearly 10% to about 5.7% as compute and networking grew to about 77% of the basket, where Europe's share is small and declining.

theme_stances.key_argument: Europe benefits from the US AI build-out in power and cooling, but its aggregate share falls as demand shifts toward computing.
theme_stances.evidence: Europe benefits, but its strengths lie outside computing
